utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all of you. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Slobodan Praljak, Milivoj Petkovic, Valentin Coric, and Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have a Status Conference this afternoon. May I ask the parties for their appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Kenneth Scott for the Prosecutor, and with me today is Ms. Josee D'Aoust, Mr. Pieter Kruger, Mr. Roeland Bos, and case manager Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. And the Defence, perhaps in the order from right to left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Zelimir Par. I am the Defence counsel for Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Zeljko Olujic. I'm a lawyer from the Republic of Croatia, and I'm defending Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm Bozidar Kovacic, Defence lawyer from Croatia, for Mr. Slobodan Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. Then the second row.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I am Defence lawyer for the fourth accused, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Tomislav Jonjic, and I defend Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Marinko Skobic, a lawyer from Mostar, and I am Defence lawyer for the accused Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skobic. We're here on a Status Conference. I received the report of a 65 ter meeting that was held yesterday. I would very much like to focus on the issues remaining since that 65 ter meeting, and I'd like to start with disclosure. The Chamber has read a lot of submissions. Sometimes perhaps not everything written in those submissions was necessary to write down because other solutions could have been found by the cooperation between the parties, but I would like to know what the remaining issues are. And if I have understood well, five out of six counsel are satisfied that the Prosecution has fulfilled its disclosure obligations, but I do understand that counsel for Mr. Petkovic, Ms. Alaburic, that you still have a matter of principle you'd like to pursue. But let me first check whether my observation in respect of the other five counsel was correct. Yes or no? Since I do not hear any denials, I take it that for counsel of Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Coric that disclosure issues are non-existing any more. Ms. Alaburic, I -- from the reading of your submissions, it appears that you're mainly concerned about the way in which translated material is available to Mr. Petkovic, and especially that you'd like it to be in -- written in hard-copy form and that the availability of audiotapes in the language of your client, Mr. Petkovic, that that does not satisfy you. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is mainly correct. If I may explain why I use the word "mainly." Yesterday there was an agreement made the complete material would be delivered to us on two CDs. I trust that we have resolved my objection referring to the provision of the supporting material in EDS which had not been available directly to the accused. I believe that the other unsolved matters to which I objected, which I deemed to be important and crucial and which I would like to summarise as follows: Firstly, the supporting material is not differentiated according to individual accused but, rather, the whole 1.700 documents were delivered as if they applied to each individual accused separately; believing that the accused in composite indictment cannot be denied the right to a fair trial, I believe that each individual accused has the right to know which part of the supporting material, in view of the OTP, supports the indictment or the part of the indictment that pertains to him particularly. My second objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask a question on this issue, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not the first case where we have several accused. Is there any case law that you rely upon to support your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the case law that I managed to consult, I only saw that there were cases when certain accused were not given the material that pertained to other accused, and therefore the request by these accused for -- that they wanted to have full insight into the material relating to the remaining accused. Unfortunately, I have no knowledge of any case that an accused in a composite indictment ever requested the supporting material to be divided as regards individual accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Thank you. I interrupted you. You were about to make your -- to summarise your second point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second objection referred to the transcript of the conversation of the first accused Prlic with the Prosecution. I think that in compliance with Rule 43(vi), this transcript should be handed over to the person who took part in the conversation as a suspect and became later an accused, and that refers to both versions, the Croatian and the English one. Given that the defender here is a co-accused must not be denied the right to the supporting material and preliminary statements in comparison with other accused, the rights of the first accused, Prlic, is equal to those enjoyed by the other accused and that they should receive this transcript of the conversation in writing. The Defence counsel received this interview in English. However, we received a videotape. My request in this respect, if I read the decision correctly, is in compliance with the ruling of the Trial Chamber II in case Prosecution versus Cermak and Markac of 26 May of this year, in which the Prosecution was ordered to, according to Rule 66(A)(i), in conjunction with Rule 43(vi), provide the accused with the transcript of the interview. And my third objection referred to the testimony by Petkovic and Praljak in three cases, and I believe that these testimonies can be treated as preliminary statement and that the rule on transcript should apply to them too. These testimonies were delivered to us only in the form of videotapes, and as inasmuch as my team and I were able to search through the EDS supporting material, we couldn't find any delivery of the transcript of either in English or in -- or B/C/S or, rather, Croatian languages. All my objections, since we resolved some of them yesterday and some in direct communication with the OTP are now basically boiled down to these three objections, which I deem to be of crucial importance and made in principle. They pertain not only to this case, but they also may apply to the rights to be exercised by other accused appearing before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. I have one specific question for you, Mr. Scott. As far as the testimonies of Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Praljak is concerned, I'm not taking any position at this moment whether these are preliminary interviews but the testimony of them, I do understand that the videotape has been provided to Ms. Alaburic. Is there any reason why the transcript of those hearings, I don't know whether they were public or not, could not be provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct, if I understand, that the testimony provided by Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Praljak in the earlier cases, these are not statements made to the OTP. They weren't statements taken by the OTP. They were trial testimony, in court, and the recordings were made as in the usual manner, and those have been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, may I just interrupt you. I said I took no position whatever, so that I'm correct in joining your position is not a fair way of dealing with the matter. I kept out of it. I said testimonies. Whether you consider them preliminary statements or not is a completely different matter. I have taken no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. I don't see any reason physically why the existing transcript, English transcript that is recorded, that is created in the course of usual business can't be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Alaburic, would that meet your third point? Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My headphones are not properly working so I'm following the English version. If you could just give me a minute to read from the transcript what exactly your question was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll be glad to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right. If I understand correctly, Mr. Scott said that they had an English transcript and that there was no reason why we should not have them. The Defence counsel would truly be grateful to the OTP if they did that. However, if this transcript should be translated into B/C/S and given to the accused will be up to the Court to decide. I would only just like to add that I know of the case law -- instances in which the trial transcripts were not given to the accused from trials. Instead, they were given videotapes. However, I believe that in this particular instance we're dealing with a completely different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, the issue of transcripts in English has been solved, and the remaining issue, whether you're entitled to have a hard translated copy, is still remaining. Ms. Alaburic, just one question. Did you ever ask Mr. Scott to receive an English copy of the transcript of Mr. Petkovic and Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott -- Mr. Scott is aware of my objections. Before I appealed to the Court with my first submission, each and every of my objections or dilemma was first explained to Mr. Scott in writing. Therefore, Mr. Scott is fully aware of my objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, first of all I would like you to respond to that and to ask whether you were aware and, if so, why not English transcripts are already in the hands of Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, and I was just checking, Your Honour, on this matter, and perhaps as a further solution or to clarify, it's our understanding -- I thought -- I thought that they were, and I've just confirmed with the case manager that in fact the English transcripts were provided by cover letter dated the 27th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then my next observation would be that if there's any possible misunderstanding, please double-check first before writing motions or further spend time on the issues in court. Ms. Alaburic, the Chamber will give a brief opportunity to Mr. Scott to respond. At the same time, I add to that I wonder whether it is necessary, because what Ms. Alaburic has done is just to summarise what's already in the written submissions. If the Prosecution would like to respond by summarising the messages, that is not necessary because the Chamber has the full information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I'll abide by the Chamber's instructions and say nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not an instruction. I just said it's not necessary, which is of course not an instruction, but I do understand that you very much value an efficient spending of the time in court. That's, then, the -- is there anything else on the disclosure issue that should be raised at this moment? Ms. Alaburic, the Chamber will give a decision in writing as soon as possible. Then we have an issue pending which only concerns Mr. Praljak but might be of some importance for the other accused as well since they are bound by the same conditions, in view of their provisional release. Did I understand you well, Mr. Kovacic, that Mr. Praljak would like to have further guidance as to how to interpret the prohibition to have contact with the media?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, your interpretation is right. We are only little bit afraid whether we as -- I mean, Defence and my client, whether we interpret -- interpreted the order inappropriately, whether the sentence "any media" includes any media in whatever the subject matter can be or only limited to these proceedings. Even -- of course we agree, even remotely - and that I'm adding after seeing the response yesterday - even if remotely connected to this case, of course the client will not enter any contact with media. But if, for example, something entirely different issue like postal stamps or sport or whatever, then we think he is entitled to talk with media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you the following guidance on the conditions, and this, of course, would apply for the accused as well. First of all, if an accused would incidentally observe the presence of the media at an occasion where he also is present, that as such is not a reason to withdraw from that event unless the media would focus their attention on the presence of the accused at that occasion. If so, the accused should, under those circumstances, withdraw. So therefore, if they're in a meeting and the media are following what is happening in the meeting, not specifically the presence of the accused, that's no problem. But as soon as everyone is, just speak in terms of the press, zooming in on the presence of the accused, then the presence of the accused gets a certain weight which should be avoided. So then the accused should leave that meeting. Whenever at such an occasion questions would be put it an accused, let's say the beginning of an interview, those questions should not be answered, and those questions would already indicate that the presence of the media is focusing, perhaps among other things, on the presence of the accused. So no -- certainly no interviews, even not if it's by just coincidental meeting with media. The accused should also avoid to attend whatever event or meeting where they could expect that the media would be present and would focus on the presence of the accused. The final issue is the one you raised about the postal stamps. It is often difficult to clearly distinguish between whether such an occasion would have no link whatsoever or whether it could be perceived in whatever way as having a link with the case. So therefore, for your guidance: If someone would present a book on postal stamps prior to going to such an event, the accused should ask permission. And if it's really just postal stamps and nothing else, then it's very likely that the permission would be given. But just to remain in the example, postal stamps are sometimes about flowers. Sometimes there are postal stamps on the organisation of the Red Cross. There may be even postal stamps which are printed in memory of historical events which are not, under all circumstances, not linked to this conflict or any other conflict or any Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond historical events. So in order to make no mistakes, usually if you publish a book on postal stamps, you know well in advance when this will be presented. You can also expect the press to be there. So under those circumstances, the accused invited to get in touch. Defence are invited to get in touch with the senior legal officer and then get a decision, not after a couple of weeks, but quickly. Is this guidance sufficiently clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For me, I think yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to tell you without having those guidelines, which of course will be very much helpful, I just wanted to stress that the client actually wants to keep his word. And very soon, coincidentally, actually, we found out there is a grey area. Perhaps we were not able to understand or what for ever reasons, but obviously it may happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate that the accused was seeking further guidance from the Chamber in order to fully observe the condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further issues in this respect? If not, then we have one matter which primarily concerns Mr. Coric. And I don't know whether we should deal with it in the presence of all other and whether the -- Mr. Jonjic, whether the subject matter as such, which is a matter of -- health-related and family circumstances is something you'd like to deal with in public session and whether you'd like to address me in private session or in the absence of other counsel. It's -- there's no direct link to the substance of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't see any reason to exclude the public, given the fact that the documents that the request by Mr. Coric is based was submitted as confidential [as interpreted]. However, the discussion about the request itself can be conducted without mentioning any particular medical circumstances that his request was based upon. Therefore, I don't see any reason for excluding the public, and I don't know if there is any need for everybody here to be burdened with this type of discussion, and by that I mean all members of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jonjic, did I understand that the Defence yesterday received guidance as to provide further detailed guarantees as to what would happen if Mr. Coric would reside for a short period of time on BH territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Last week, in the communication with the senior legal advisor, Mr. Harhoff, I was given an instruction to appeal for additional guarantees to be provided by the government of BH, and already today we have the appropriate documents in hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can then soon accept further submissions by you in relation to this issue and the Chamber will give a ruling when the Prosecution has had an opportunity to respond to the last information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Prosecution is invited, in view of the subject matter, to respond as quickly as possible to any further submissions by Mr. Jonjic, because delays here are to be avoided. Then we have an issue on protection of victims and witnesses. There have been some suggestions by the Office of the Prosecutor how to deal with it. Is there any need, in addition to what has been written down, to address the Chamber in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, ever so briefly. And primarily on the -- what appears to be sound advice of your senior legal officer, Mr. Harhoff yesterday. The issue was discussed, and as I understand -- as I understand it, and I'm sure I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, there was ultimately no Defence objection to our proposal. Mr. Harhoff thought perhaps the best way of resolving it for the record was an oral motion on the record in this fashion, and it concerns this: On the 30 this is of July, the Chamber entered its order for protective measures. In paragraph 2, and I won't take the time to read it, but paragraph 2 essentially requires that the Prosecution, in the course of making its disclosures, distinguish in all instances between public and non-public material. I've explained to both Mr. Harhoff and to counsel that in reality, and perhaps the Chamber won't be surprised, that is a substantial burden on the Prosecution. There is, despite the modern -- the wonders, excuse me, the wonders of modern technology, the is no one-button fix by which we can simply sort out the public versus the non-public. It's a very labour-intensive process. Further, it's our understanding, and perhaps there is where there might have been some previous misunderstanding, the OTP has always operated on the assumption or the premise that Defence counsel have the right to make use in a reasonable and discreet way of any material provided to them, whether it's public or non-public, as long as it's for legitimate defence usage and provided they do so in a reasonably discreet manner. It was clear in talking to Mr. Harhoff, which was very helpful, that once we understood that was the understanding and the Defence is not in any way -- according to our understanding -- barred from using even the non-public material in such a fashion, the reason for that requirement seemed to largely go away, in light -- and in contrast or especially in light of the considerable burden placed on the Prosecution. So we, Your Honour, would move, if I might and I'll certainly respond to the Chamber's further questions, but for purposes of the record, the Prosecution would move to amend the order for protective measures dated 30 July 2004, to remove paragraph 2, which of course would require other paragraphs, I suppose, to be renumbered. And we would also note that as to paragraph number 4, there would have to be some changes because there's some premise -- there are some things in paragraph 4 that reflect on with paragraph 2, that talk about public versus non-public. The Prosecution clearly does believe, and we don't wish to be misunderstood on this point, that indeed as to all material disclosed to the Defence -- essentially all of it, except, I suppose, for truly open-source material, newspaper articles, it's all sensitive to one degree or another, witness statements, et cetera and it's only to be used of course for legitimate purposes of preparing the case. And that would apply to all categories and the Defence would be expected to use the material discreetly and with appropriate safeguards in all cases. But paragraph 4, we would suggest respectfully, would probably also have some amended to make it consistent with the removal of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. The Defence is concerned, I would like to know if any Defence counsel would not agree with Mr. Scott on the issue of discretion and appropriate safeguards in all cases. If there would be anything else, apart from this point where on the basis of the silence I take it that you all agree -- if there's any other response to be made? If not, we'll proceed to our next subject. Again, I interpret your collective silence to move on to the next subject. A decision will be made, Mr. Scott. We'll have to review the 30th July decision so as in order to avoid any inconsistencies, if we would follow your oral motion. Then on my agenda is agreement on facts. I do understand that the matter has been discussed with the senior legal officer, Mr. Harhoff, and that the parties are still working on it. Yes. The Chamber would not only encourage the parties to work on it but also to see whether they can achieve a substantive result. Is there anything you'd like to raise in respect of this subject? If not, we'll proceed to the next point that is on the agenda, that's the pre-trial work plan. I do understand that a plan has been more or less agreed upon, at least in a calendar where the first 65 ter meeting will take place on the 15th of December, and then the next one on the 14th of February. A more detailed work plan will be prepared. So that's not only dates that are set, because that's certainly helpful, but it's also certainly not sufficient to make the necessary progress. Is there any matter to be raised in view of the health of the accused or -- at this moment? I remember that one of your clients had some difficulty in walking and sitting for a longer time. Is there any positive or negative development in that? These were back problems, isn't it -- isn't it, Mr. Skobic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SKOBIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. Accused Pusic did experience different problems, but since he is provisionally in Zagreb, a place where adequate medical assistance is available, his condition is now completely satisfactory, although he is undergoing a permanent course of treatment; but he doesn't have any major problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skobic. I'm glad to hear that medical treatment has a positive effect. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will raise the issue of a time limit for the preliminary motions. I do understand that it has been discussed yesterday and that all parties would accept preliminary motions to be filed not any later than the 15th of December. And I also understand, but please, Ms. Alaburic, correct me if I'm wrong, that the matters of principle you'd like to raise do not affect as such your ability to file a pre-trial -- the preliminary motions, if you intend to file one or more of them. Yes, from --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your understanding is correct, Your Honour. I will fully abide by the deadlines we agreed upon yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence counsel have also understood that the Chamber, until now, has not given any permission to go beyond the ten-page limit; but at the same time, the Chamber has made clear that preliminary motions on different subjects would each have ten pages. They can be filed separately. So therefore, whether it's jurisdiction or whether it's the form of the indictment, you would have on each of the subjects -- I'm not encouraging you to use on each of these subjects the full ten pages, but on one subject you're limited to ten pages. And you're certainly aware that in the directive it's also clearly indicated what is within the ten pages and what is not and what's the size of the letters you can use and number of lines. Is there any other issue you'd like to raise at this moment? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I pushed it but not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I'm a bit wrong, but I just wanted to add, very briefly, a very few words on the issue of undisputed facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Personally, I believe that it is a perfect tool which may seriously contribute to a more efficient trial. However, I don't want to leave an image and false hope of all of us in this courtroom that this process will go very fast and very soon. This simply cannot happen, Your Honour. For time being, of course, because I don't see any possibility to discuss undisputed facts before we know what actually will be indictment, because the indictment we are dealing now with are not giving us a chance even to run some basic defence investigations. In other words, a usual calendar of work or plan of work for Defence is a little bit change. I first have to see what ultimately the indictment looks like, and only then I can decide which material first I need from the other cases connected on one way or another and where I'm going into my own Defence investigations. Of course, I have to learn the facts. And within facts I have to distinguish which of the facts will be disputed, which of them will not be disputed, and only then I can enter into the process of trying to -- of stipulation. The plan was I would initiate this because it's easier for one who is starting with the proposals. I just want you to have a clear picture that despite of our wish, my wish at least, this process, by my humble opinion, cannot even start before we see indictment, we see other facts. So we are not just about to start. That is my only remark, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further submissions to be made? Now, Mr. Kovacic, I'll respond immediately to your observation just made. I do understand that it's your expectation that the indictment will look different in the future, which of course still is to be -- we'll first have to wait whether the indictment as it stands now will be the one that stands in the future, of course. I can't say anything about that, because we'd first have to see whether any preliminary motions on the form of the indictment. But the Chamber expects all Defence counsel to start working on the basis of the indictment as it is now. So therefore, you should focus your activities on the indictment as it is. And of course I can imagine that you say, "Well, I have a specific part of the indictment which I'll challenge as to the appropriateness of its form," but I hardly can imagine that there are not considerable portions you could not yet start to investigate, and as a consequence of such investigations, that you could not start, not enter into whatever conversations with the OTP as far as an agreement on facts is concerned. Of course, agreement on facts is always within the limits of your responsibility to defend the accused. But this is a clear mark that if at a later stage you say, "Well, even though the indictment has been slightly changed, we could not start until the moment we knew," then the answer will be that you should have started only the basis of the indictment as it stood then. Of course we'll see if the whole of the indictment will change. Of course the situation would be a bit different, and you would be excused for not being properly prepared at that time. But if the changes would not be basic ones, and if the changes were be foreseen by yourself on the basis of the preliminary motions you are about to file, then all the remaining part should be something you should start working at. This is a brief response to the observations you must made. Is there any other issue you'd like to raise, either Prosecution or Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on the issue of the Rule 75(A) motions, we would probably feel more comfortable if it was made clear on the record: Our understanding was it's also agreed yesterday -- and I assume or I hope Mr. Harhoff would have communicated this to you, I'm sure he has -- that in turn the Prosecution responses would be due on the 28th of January in light of the end of the year holidays, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I only mentioned the first time limit, but I did understand that it has been agreed, and the Chamber also affirms the date you just mentioned for the response of the Prosecution as the 28th of January, 2005. Any further issues to be raised? If not, this concludes this Status Conference. I thank you very much for assisting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 4.03 p.m.
